title: Personal Goal-Setting
keyIdea: A wish is "I want to get better". A goal says exactly what you will do, how you will measure it, and by when, and it is a stretch you can really reach. Plan the steps and what you will do when something gets in the way, track your progress against the plan, and when it stops working, change the plan before you give up on the goal.

kid: "Get better at swimming" is a wish. You can never tell when you have done it. A goal is sharper: "Swim 25 metres front crawl without stopping by the end of term." It is specific (what exactly), measurable (a number you can check) and has a time frame (by when).
Pick a goal that is a stretch. It should be harder than what you do now, but not so big that you give up. If you read 2 books a month, 3 or 4 is a stretch. Twenty is too big for now.

Things will get in your way, so plan for them. Use an if–then plan: "If it rains on my running day, then I will skip indoors for 10 minutes." Then track your progress each week. Write down what you did and compare it with your plan.
If you fall behind, do not give up. Ask why. Then change the plan: a new time, extra practice on the hard part, or a smaller step. Only make the goal smaller if it really is too big.
adult: Children aged 9 to 11 learn to set realistic personal goals, plan steps, check progress and adjust. This sits in the IB PYP Personal, Social and Physical Education strand (identity) and in UK PSHE work on self-esteem and aspiration. Useful terms are specific, measurable, realistic (achievable) and time frame, often taught as SMART. Add short-term and long-term goals, steps, obstacles, progress and review.

Research backs three habits. Specific, fairly hard goals lead to more effort than "do your best" (Locke and Latham's goal-setting theory). If–then plans, called implementation intentions (Gollwitzer), make children far more likely to act when an obstacle comes. And regular progress checks, best when written down, help people stick with a goal (Harkin and colleagues, 2016).

Watch for common mistakes. Goals are vague ("be better at maths"), too big ("every times table by tomorrow") or have no date. There is no plan for obstacles. Progress is checked only at the deadline, and a slow week is treated as failure. The other slip is giving up the goal when it is the plan that needs to change. Model saying: "That didn't work. What will I try instead?"

In the lab your child sharpens a vague goal into a specific, measurable one with a time frame. They set a goal size in the stretch zone, match obstacles to if–then plans, log weeks of reading against a plan line, and choose the best change when progress stalls.

familyTip: Pick one goal together for the next four weeks, such as a skill or a book series. Write it as "I will ___ by ___", add one if–then plan, and put a simple tick chart on the fridge. Check it every Sunday and ask: "On track? If not, what will we change?"

visual.caption: Is each one a sharp goal or a vague wish? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Read 3 chapter books by half term
Learn my 8 times table by Friday
Run 1 km without stopping by May
Be good at drawing one day
Practise piano 10 minutes a day for 4 weeks

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sharpen a vague goal, set a stretch-size goal, match obstacles to if–then plans, track weeks against a plan and choose how to adjust.

practice.prompt: Which is a specific, measurable goal with a time frame?
choices: Score 18 out of 20 on my spelling test by the end of the month
Do lots of spelling one day
practice.hint: Can you check it with a number and a date?
practice.explain: 18 out of 20 is measurable, spelling test is specific, and the end of the month is the time frame. The others are wishes.

practice.prompt: Ava can do {n} skips in a row. Which goal is a good stretch for next week?
practice.hint: A stretch is a bit harder than now, but realistic.
practice.explain: {=n+5} is harder than {n} but reachable in a week. {n} is no stretch, and {=n*20} is too big for now.

practice.prompt: Which is an if–then plan for an obstacle?
choices: If I am tired after school, then I practise for just 5 minutes
practice.hint: It names the problem and what you will do about it.
practice.explain: "If tired, then 5 minutes" decides the action before the problem comes. Trying hard and hoping are not plans.

practice.prompt: Your plan is {p} pages a week. After 2 weeks you have read {=2*p-20} pages. Are you on track?
practice.explain: The plan for 2 weeks is {=2*p} pages and you have read {=2*p-20}. You are 20 pages behind, so it is time to check why.

practice.prompt: You keep missing your piano practice because you do it late at night when you are sleepy. What is the best change?
choices: Keep the same time and try harder
practice.hint: The goal is fine. What is the real problem?
practice.explain: The problem is the time, so change the plan. Giving up drops the goal, and the same plan gives the same result.

pool.prompt: What turns a wish into a goal?
choices: Saying exactly what, how you will measure it and by when
pool.hint: Think specific, measurable and time frame.
pool.explain: A goal is specific, measurable and has a time frame, so you can plan for it and check it.

pool.prompt: Which goal has no time frame?
pool.hint: Look for words that say by when, like a date or a number of weeks.
pool.explain: "Swim 50 m backstroke" is specific and measurable, but it says nothing about when.

pool.prompt: Sam can juggle {n} times. Which goal is too big for this month?
pool.hint: Too big means so hard you may give up.
pool.explain: {=n*50} is far beyond {n} in a month, so it is likely to feel hopeless. {=n+4} or {=n+8} is a stretch.

pool.prompt: Obstacle: "My little brother wants to play when I do homework." Which is the if–then plan?
choices: If he asks, then I say I will play after 20 minutes
I will try to ignore him
pool.hint: An if–then plan says: if this happens, then I will do this exact thing.
pool.explain: It names the obstacle and a clear action. "Try to ignore" is vague and the last one is not a plan.

pool.prompt: Why track your progress each week instead of only at the deadline?
choices: So you spot problems while there is time to fix them
pool.hint: What can you do if you find out you are behind early?
pool.explain: Weekly checks show when you fall behind, so you can change the plan in time.

pool.prompt: You planned {k} maths problems a day. You have done that every day this week. What does that show?
pool.hint: Compare what you did with the plan.
pool.explain: Doing {k} a day, as planned, means you are on track. Keep going, and review at the end of the next week.

pool.prompt: Your times-table scores have not gone up for 2 weeks. What should you do first?
choices: Find which facts you miss and practise those
Do the same test again and again
pool.hint: Find out why it is not working.
pool.explain: Look for the weak part and change how you practise. Repeating the same thing gives the same result.

pool.prompt: When is it right to make a goal smaller?
choices: When it is too big to fit your life, even with a good plan
As soon as it feels hard
pool.hint: Feeling hard is normal for a stretch.
pool.explain: A stretch should feel hard. Shrink the goal only if it is not realistic, for example if it leaves no time for other things.
